strengths: The paper identifies a relevant dual-use threat: fine-tuned LLMs can form persistent covert channels even when ordinary network egress is restricted. Distinguishing channel effectiveness, payload recoverability, and detectability is conceptually useful.

The embedding-hyperplane construction is simple and moderately original. Its keyed vocabulary partition is compatible with ordinary constrained generation, and the experiments cover two 8B model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B LoRA setting, two training distributions, and out-of-distribution prompts.

Several configurations improve 32-bit exact-match accuracy over ASCII-plus-parity, including 17% to 30% for Llama-8B LoRA, 24% to 43% for Ministral-8B LoRA, and 9% to 19% for Llama-70B LoRA. The paper also reports failures and mixed OOD generalization rather than presenting uniformly favorable results.

The presentation is generally clear and well organized. The appendix supplies training hyperparameters, probe architectures, data splits, metric definitions, and derivations, making the experimental design easier to inspect.

The limitations and impact discussion appropriately acknowledges white-box access requirements, possible adaptive attacks against probes, and the offensive nature of the contribution. Coordinating disclosure of attack code while releasing defensive code is a reasonable ethical precaution.
weaknesses: The central detection evidence does not establish a steganography detector. Every prompt contains the secret in plaintext, so probes can recover information already present in the input. Comparing maliciously fine-tuned models only against base models cannot distinguish a covert channel from ordinary fine-tuning that increases attention to or retention of the supplied string. The paper needs benign fine-tuning controls matched in data, optimization, and secret-bearing prompts, plus an actual model-level detection evaluation with specificity, false-positive rates, multiple independently trained models, and held-out attack keys.

The claimed keyless recoverability metric is not operationally aligned with the threat model. The R_bucket classifiers are trained with ground-truth bucket bits, but a defender lacking the key generally does not possess those labels. Moreover, recoverability is defined relative to a small, selected set of XGBoost/MLP classifiers rather than as an intrinsic security property. Results use only one reported bucket seed (42), provide no comprehensive numerical table or uncertainty analysis for Figure 2, and therefore do not support broad claims of resistance to reverse engineering.

The theoretical argument about perplexity is materially invalid for the stated conclusion. Theorem 7.2 is a lower bound on a surrogate involving the fine-tuned model's probability of the base model's top token; the empirical perplexity instead scores generated text under the base model. More fundamentally, a lower bound approaching two does not prove that a channel carrying arbitrarily many bits can attain perplexity near two. Thus it cannot support the claim that large payloads can be hidden within normal fine-tuning ranges.

The numerical interpretation of the KL result is also unsupported. For 1,024 buckets, the text assumes that whenever the target bucket excludes the top token, its best token has probability 0.3. Only one bucket can contain that second-ranked token; most target buckets will have much lower-probability representatives and potentially much larger promotion cost. The derivation should average the bucket-dependent optimum rather than reuse the same two-token example for all 1,023 non-top buckets.

The XOR experiment is not a convincing 'non-decodable' control. Its output remains a deterministic 32-bit function of the secret, and the asserted circularity is not a proof of non-recoverability. Failure of the chosen classifiers under limited data shows only empirical difficulty for those classifiers. It does not isolate steganographic internal traces, especially because probes still observe activations conditioned on a plaintext secret.

Attack effectiveness is incomplete and inconsistently strong: many exact-match rates remain below 50%, several embedding variants underperform the parity baseline, and OOD accuracy is often near zero. Per-bit error rates, effective channel capacity, error-correcting-code baselines, training-seed variability, and comparisons under equal data and generation budgets are missing. Relative improvements such as 123% also overemphasize gains from very low baselines.

The text-quality study is too small to support imperceptibility claims: coherence and stability use only 10 prompts and KL uses 20, with no human evaluation or benign fine-tuning control. The assertion that observed KL/perplexity values fall within 'typical' fine-tuning ranges is not validated on matched models and tasks.

Reproducibility is only partial. Important generation and classifier settings, seed-level training variation, preprocessing details, model checkpoints, compute requirements, and underlying numeric results are absent. The paper promises future release of detection code while apparently withholding attack code, so the reported results cannot presently be independently reproduced.

Overall, the geometric attack is promising, but the keyless-security evidence, mechanistic detection claim, and theoretical justification for the inadequacy of distributional steganalysis each have central soundness problems. These issues require substantial new controls and corrected theory rather than a minor revision.

strengths: The paper studies an important security problem: persistent covert channels introduced through malicious LLM fine-tuning, including both attack construction and white-box detection.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. The threat model, geometric construction, experimental configurations, and principal results are easy to follow.

The empirical study covers two 8B model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B configuration, multiple datasets, and out-of-distribution prompts. Table 1 shows genuine attack-side improvements over the parity baseline in several settings, especially for LoRA models.
The separation of token-to-bucket inference from bucket-to-secret decoding is conceptually useful, even though the proposed operational metrics do not yet support the claimed security conclusions.

The paper includes hyperparameters, probe architectures, data splits, uncertainty estimates for several results, a limitations discussion, and a reasonable dual-use impact statement with planned responsible disclosure.
weaknesses: The central low-recoverability claim is not established. R_bucket and R_secret are defined as maxima over classifier families, but experimentally approximated using only a small set of supervised models under an unclear analyst-data model. These measurements are neither cryptographic security guarantees nor convincing estimates of an optimal keyless adversary.

The evaluation is particularly unfavorable to the most natural recovery attack. Embedding inputs are PCA-reduced from the full embedding dimension to 50 dimensions, even though the proposed bucket assignment is exactly a linear hyperplane in the full embedding space. A linear classifier on unreduced embeddings is omitted; PCA can discard the seed direction and artificially create the reported low recoverability. Conversely, if bucket labels are unavailable, it is unclear how any of the supervised recovery classifiers would be trained. This ambiguity is fundamental.

Security appears to rest on obscurity of random seeds rather than a characterized key space or cryptographic construction. The paper uses a fixed bucketing seed of 42, supplies no sample-complexity or adaptive recovery analysis, and does not evaluate seed recovery, chosen-secret queries, clustering, or white-box attacks despite granting the defender model inspection and query access. A keyed random hash baseline is also missing, so the benefit of learned embedding geometry over a generic keyed partition is not isolated.

The detection experiments do not demonstrate a detector with controlled false-positive behavior. The secret is explicitly present in every probe prompt, including for the base model, and probes are trained separately to recover it from activations. Higher recoverability after malicious fine-tuning may simply show increased attention to the supplied secret. There are no benign fine-tuned controls, no model-level detection rule or threshold, and no evaluation across independently trained benign and malicious checkpoints.

The claimed gray-box detection still requires 1,000 prompts with known secrets, access to internal activations, a corresponding clean base model, and supervised regression targets. It therefore does not match the broad claim that internal signatures provide an actionable general detector. Several results are also exceptions: Embedding+Embedding bit probes often show little separation, and Ministral full fine-tuning can have embedding-recovery scores at or below the base model.

The theoretical section does not support its stated conclusion. Theorem 7.2 analyzes Q's probability of the base distribution's argmax token, which is not the perplexity metric defined in Appendix E. Moreover, a lower bound approaching two does not by itself establish that a trainable steganographic model can achieve perplexity near two. The KL illustration assumes that the second-most-probable token is the required token for non-top buckets, which is incompatible with a random 1,024-bucket partition in general. Neither bound is validated against realistic token distributions or learned models.

Claims that distributional steganalysis is ineffective are therefore too strong. Figure 4 provides no matched benign-fine-tuning controls, while symmetric KL values around 11–14 are asserted to be normal mainly by citation. Without comparable benign checkpoints or an actual detector ROC, the experiments cannot establish indistinguishability from ordinary fine-tuning.

Attack effectiveness remains limited and uneven: many exact-recovery rates are only 19–43%, several embedding variants underperform the baseline, and Table 2 shows severe prompt-distribution dependence, including near-zero transfer in many configurations. Relative improvements such as 123% magnify small absolute changes such as 9% to 19%. Results apparently do not include independent training runs, so robustness to training randomness is uncertain.

The utility evaluation is too small and indirect for the deployment claims. Coherence and stability use only 10 prompts and KL only 20; there is no human evaluation, instruction-following/task-success measurement, or representative benign fine-tuning baseline. Semantic similarity between adjacent sentences does not establish that the compromised model still performs its intended task convincingly.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the secret-encoding hyperplane seeds, several classifier/XGBoost settings, exact generation and sampling procedures, compute details, and trained checkpoints are not supplied, while code release is only promised. The paper's polished presentation and honest acknowledgment of white-box limitations do not compensate for the unsupported central recoverability and detection claims.

strengths: The paper studies an important and credible security threat: persistent covert channels implanted through LLM fine-tuning. Distinguishing detection from payload recovery is conceptually useful.

The embedding-space bucketing construction is simple, intuitive, and reasonably original in this training-time setting. The experiments span two model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B model, disjoint secrets, and out-of-distribution prompts.

The attack evaluation reports exact 32-bit recovery rather than only average bit accuracy. Table 1 shows substantial improvements in several difficult LoRA settings, including 17% to 30%, 24% to 43%, and 9% to 19%.

The presentation is generally clear and well organized. The appendices document training hyperparameters, probe architectures, sample counts, and metric definitions, while the main text openly reports negative cases and limited OOD generalization.

The dual-use implications are recognized, with responsible disclosure and asymmetric code-release plans. The paper also appropriately acknowledges that its detector requires hidden-state access and may be evaded by adaptive training.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central low-recoverability evidence is not convincing. The bucket rule is exactly a linear threshold in the model's accessible embedding space, yet the evaluation first projects embeddings to only 50 PCA dimensions and tests a small menu of XGBoost/MLP models. Discarding most embedding dimensions can manufacture apparent difficulty and does not support the maximization over classifier families in Definition 3.1. A full-dimensional linear probe is the most natural omitted attack. Moreover, the empirical classifiers receive supervised true bucket/secret labels, but the threat model does not explain how a keyless defender obtains such labels or how many labeled observations are assumed.

Soundness: Appendix D explicitly gives the embedding-bucketing seed as 42. If this seed and the construction are available to the defender, the purported secret partition is directly reconstructible and R_bucket is 100%. If 42 is not intended to be disclosed, the paper needs a proper key-generation and key-secrecy model, seed entropy, sample-complexity analysis, and evaluation against key/partition recovery attacks. A large unspecified seed-search space is not a security argument.

Soundness: the proposed mechanistic method is not evaluated as a detector. Probes are trained separately with labeled secrets and compared only between a base model and maliciously fine-tuned models whose prompts contain those secrets in plaintext. The experiments therefore establish increased linear accessibility of a known input feature, not reliable classification of whether an unknown model is steganographic. There are no benign fine-tuned controls, model-level decision rule, held-out attack keys, false-positive rates, or adaptive attackers. Ordinary task fine-tuning could produce the same base-to-fine-tuned gap.

Soundness: the theoretical section does not justify the broad conclusion that substantial payloads are achievable within normal fine-tuning drift. The 10-bit KL example assumes that the required bucket's best token is always the base model's second-ranked token, whereas under 1,024 random buckets it will generally be much lower ranked. The theorem is a conditional minimum for a selected target token, and a lower bound alone does not establish the claimed achievable divergence under realistic bucket assignments. The perplexity result evaluates probability of the base model's argmax token rather than standard data-distribution perplexity and relies on an argmax tie that may not transmit the required token.

Evidence: the claim that KL divergence and perplexity are uninformative under ordinary fine-tuning lacks matched benign fine-tuning baselines. Figure 4 uses only 10 prompts for coherence/stability and 20 for KL, provides no human or task-quality evaluation, and compares its values to loosely cited 'heavy fine-tuning' ranges rather than identically trained benign controls. This is insufficient to conclude that standard steganalysis is ineffective.

Evidence: attack improvements are inconsistent across configurations. Several embedding variants underperform ASCII+Parity, sometimes materially, and many OOD exact-match rates are near zero. Relative improvements such as 123% amplify small absolute changes from 9% to 19%; the practical exfiltration channel remains unreliable in several highlighted settings.

The XOR experiment does not prove that output information has been removed. The mask is a deterministic function of a secret drawn from only 26^4 possibilities, so non-decodability requires a precise hidden-key assumption and analysis; 'circularity' and failure of the chosen classifiers do not establish negligible information or computational security.

Reproducibility is only partial: many training details are supplied, but code is merely promised, the recoverability experiment omits essential dataset sizes and exact classifier/output formulation, confidence intervals and aggregation are not consistently defined, and constrained-generation/sampling details are incomplete. These omissions are especially important because the headline security findings depend strongly on the attacker model and classifier capacity.

Significance and originality are promising but currently limited by the above validation gaps. Random-hyperplane partitioning is closely related to cited watermarking ideas, while the more novel detection claim lacks the benign controls needed to make it actionable. The attack experiments remain useful preliminary evidence, but the unsupported central security and detection claims prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality: The paper presents a creative embedding-geometry construction for both secret encoding and vocabulary bucketing, extending training-time LLM steganography beyond token-ID parity.
Significance: Covert exfiltration by fine-tuned models is an important safety problem, and distinguishing detectability from payload recoverability is a useful conceptual direction.

Sound empirical scope: The attack study covers two 8B architectures, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B LoRA model, multiple encoding/bucketing combinations, held-out secrets, out-of-distribution prompts, mixed-motive training, capability benchmarks, temperature robustness, and retokenization noise.

The mixed-motive experiments are valuable: they show that ordinary instruction data can partially restore capability without eliminating the covert behavior, making the threat model more realistic than purely malicious fine-tuning.

Presentation: The paper is generally readable, motivates the attack/defense structure clearly, and provides useful diagrams, tables, appendices, and an honest limitations section covering payload scale, capability degradation, encoding scalability, and white-box access.

Ethics: The dual-use risk is explicitly acknowledged, attack-code release is conditioned on responsible disclosure, and the manuscript does not conceal the substantial capability degradation and deployment assumptions.
weaknesses: Soundness—the central theoretical detection argument is not established. Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 are lower bounds on divergence/perplexity, whereas the claim that large payloads can be hidden with small shift requires an achievable upper bound or construction under realistic token distributions. A small lower bound does not imply that a small value is attainable.

The numerical KL example is invalid for the stated uniform 1024-bucket setting: it assumes that the best token in every non-top required bucket has probability 0.3, although only one bucket can contain that second-ranked token. Most required buckets would have much lower-probability representatives and potentially far larger KL cost. This undermines the headline claim that 10 bits per token require only about 0.026 nats.

Theorem 7.2 uses an unconventional 'perplexity' based only on the base model's argmax token rather than corpus tokens or samples from the base distribution. Its near-2 bound therefore does not demonstrate preserved language quality, and the proposed 50/50 distribution may promote an extremely implausible token.

The recoverability definition is underspecified and does not cleanly match the keyless threat model. Estimating R_bucket with supervised token-to-bit labels and R_secret with secret labels gives the evaluator information that a keyless observer may not possess. Conversely, maximizing only over a few XGBoost/MLP configurations cannot justify low recoverability against a capable attacker. Query budget, known-plaintext access, sample complexity, and direct hyperplane/seed-recovery attacks are not evaluated.

The claimed security intuition is weak: the bucket rule is a linear separator in embeddings, the construction is public, and all experiments use one reported seed (42). Results across many independently sampled secret keys, stronger linear/geometric recovery attacks, and adaptive attackers are necessary before concluding that the channel resists reverse engineering.

The proposed probing method is not yet a validated detector. It trains probes separately with labeled plaintext secrets and compares representation decodability between a base and a known fine-tuned model; it does not produce or evaluate a model-level decision rule under unknown attack status. There are no benign fine-tuning controls, false-positive rates, cross-model/key transfer tests, or adaptive attacks trained to suppress the probe signal.

Because the secret appears verbatim in every probe prompt, both base and attacked models naturally represent it. Increased probe accuracy may reflect altered retention or prompt conditioning rather than a steganography-specific signature. Controls involving benign objectives that require retaining the same prompt field are especially important.

Some reported results are internally difficult to reconcile. Appendix Table 7 defines exact match as all 32 bits correct, yet Ministral Full E+E reports exact-match rates exceeding mean bit accuracy (56.7% versus 53.1% at T=0 and 53.4% versus 50.0% at T=0.7), which is impossible under that definition. This needs correction or a precise alternative definition.

Statistical evidence is incomplete. Most model fine-tuning configurations appear to use a single training run; Figure 2 lacks readily interpretable numerical values and uncertainty; recoverability dataset sizes and detailed XGBoost settings are absent; and many comparisons emphasize relative gains from low baselines despite modest absolute exact-recovery rates.

Reproducibility is only partial. Training hyperparameters are documented, but exact data-generation procedures, classifier configurations, evaluation harness details, checkpoints, and complete code are unavailable. The paper promises detection-code release while withholding attack code, which is ethically understandable but still limits independent verification.

Presentation could be tightened: several figures are dense and small, terminology alternates between detection, bit prediction, and secret recovery, and the manuscript sometimes overstates evidence—for example, calling distributional steganalysis ineffective rather than showing only that the evaluated metrics are inconclusive under selected settings.

Overall, the empirical attack study is promising, but flaws in the theoretical argument, recoverability evaluation, and validation of the proposed detector affect central claims rather than peripheral details. Substantial revision and stronger controls are required before the contribution can be reliably built upon.

strengths: Significance: The paper studies an important and timely security problem: persistent covert exfiltration by maliciously fine-tuned LLMs, including both attack and defense perspectives.

Originality: Replacing token-ID parity with seed-dependent hyperplane partitions of embedding space is a sensible extension of TrojanStego. The separation between bucket recoverability and secret recoverability is also a potentially useful conceptual distinction.

Empirical scope: The experiments cover two 8B model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B LoRA setting, multiple encoding/bucketing combinations, in-distribution and cross-prompt evaluation, capability benchmarks, mixed-motive training, temperature robustness, and retokenization noise.

Presentation and limitations: The main construction is clearly explained and illustrated, and the appendices provide substantial implementation detail. The paper candidly reports severe capability degradation, limited payload size, prompt/trigger assumptions, scaling limitations, and the white-box nature of its detection method.
Ethics: The dual-use risk is explicitly acknowledged, with a proposed responsible-disclosure process for attack code. No unresolved human-subject or dataset-consent issue is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—recoverability: The proposed metric does not establish low recoverability against a capable defender. The reported values are maxima over only four chosen classifiers, not over realistic adversaries. More seriously, bucket labels are generated by a linear hyperplane in the original embedding space, yet the evaluation discards most of that structure through 50-dimensional PCA and uses XGBoost/MLPs rather than testing a linear separator on the full embeddings. Given known token/bit pairs, the actual hidden hyperplane should be directly learnable. Thus Figure 2 may primarily demonstrate weakness of the selected attacks.

Soundness—security by seed secrecy: The construction's protection rests on an unknown random seed rather than a cryptographic argument or a measured seed-recovery attack. Appendix D even fixes the experimental bucketing seed to 42. The paper neither specifies a defensible key-generation/key-space model nor evaluates known-plaintext, chosen-prompt, hyperplane-recovery, or brute-force adversaries. Claims such as 'unrecoverable' and 'only allowing exact decoding with a shared key' are consequently much stronger than the evidence.

Soundness—theory: The KL and perplexity results do not support the stated conclusion. They are lower bounds on the cost of enforcing an argmax, so a small lower bound does not show that a feasible attack attains small divergence. The 10-bit numerical example additionally treats the second-most-probable token as the best token for essentially every one of 1023 non-top buckets, which is not true for a vocabulary partition. The perplexity theorem evaluates Q on the base model's top token rather than the manuscript's empirical perplexity definition, and a lower bound approaching two is incorrectly discussed as though perplexity is guaranteed to approach two. These issues undermine the central claim that arbitrarily large payloads can be hidden within ordinary fine-tuning drift.

Soundness—detection: Secret-recovery probes are not an operational detector. The evaluation trains separate supervised probes using 1,000 prompts whose secrets are explicitly provided in plaintext, then compares maliciously fine-tuned models only with untouched base models. There are no benign fine-tuned controls, matched models with comparable capability/distribution shift, model-level detection accuracy, false-positive rates, or held-out attack mechanisms. The measured gap can therefore arise from generic fine-tuning or increased persistence of prompt information rather than a steganography-specific signature.

Soundness—attack realism: Exact recovery remains modest in many emphasized LoRA cases (19–43% for a synthetic four-letter secret), and OOD transfer is highly prompt-distribution dependent, with many full-fine-tuned configurations near zero. Even mixed-motive models lose roughly 3–12 benchmark points in most usable settings, while Ministral full fine-tuning loses about 20–25 points. These conspicuous capability losses weaken the deployment threat model.

Evaluation: Text quality is estimated from only 10 prompts for coherence/stability and 20 for KL, without human evaluation or matched benign fine-tuning baselines. The assertion that the observed perplexity/KL shifts are 'typical' is therefore not convincingly established. Relative percentage improvements such as 123% also overstate practical gains from very low baselines.

Statistical reliability and reproducibility: Most results appear to come from a single fine-tuning run per configuration; three train/test splits of downstream probes do not capture training variance. Several confidence intervals round to zero, Table 1 does not clearly define its ± values, and Figure 2 lacks uncertainty. Hyperparameters are documented reasonably well, but exact generated datasets, checkpoints, evaluation code, and attack code are not supplied in the manuscript; the latter is deferred to responsible disclosure, limiting independent verification.

Originality and significance: Random-hyperplane embedding partitions closely resemble established semantic watermarking/bucketing ideas, and the detection component applies standard linear probing. Either could still be useful, but the paper does not sufficiently establish novelty relative to watermark key-recovery and probing-based backdoor detection literature. Because the key security and detection claims are unsupported by appropriate adversaries and controls, the current contribution is not reliable enough for acceptance.

Presentation: The paper is generally readable, but terminology repeatedly overclaims the evidence ('unrecoverable,' 'detection,' and 'proved bounds showing that large payloads can be hidden'). Some tables and multi-panel figures are very dense, and the distinction among classifier access assumptions, known plaintext, knowledge of the encoding family, and knowledge of the seed needs a much sharper threat-model treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored security problem: persistent covert channels introduced through malicious fine-tuning. The embedding-hyperplane construction is simple and effective. Across several configurations it improves exact recovery over ASCII+Parity, including 17% to 30% for Llama-8B LoRA, 24% to 43% for Ministral-8B LoRA, and 9% to 19% for Llama-70B LoRA.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: two model families, 8B and 70B scales, LoRA and full fine-tuning, multiple encoding/bucketing combinations, OOD prompt styles, mixed-motive training, capability benchmarks, temperature robustness, and retokenization effects.

The mixed-motive experiments are valuable because they expose the severe capability degradation of steganography-only training and show that LoRA models can recover much of that capability without eliminating the covert channel.

The mechanistic-probing experiments, including the secret-conditioned XOR control, provide promising evidence that malicious fine-tuning can increase the linear accessibility of secret-related information in late layers.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with extensive methodological appendices, explicit limitations, and a responsible dual-use discussion. Coordinated release of attack code while releasing detection code is an appropriate ethical precaution.
weaknesses: The central claim of low recoverability is supported only against four selected XGBoost/MLP configurations. No adaptive seed search, clustering, cryptanalytic attack, sample-complexity curve, or weight-based reverse engineering is evaluated, despite the defender being assumed to inspect the model. The classifier-training sample count is also not reported. Consequently, the experiments establish low recoverability for particular learned decoders, not that the keyed channel is meaningfully difficult to reverse-engineer.

The theoretical argument about conventional steganalysis is not sound as presented. Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 are lower bounds, which alone do not demonstrate that low KL divergence or perplexity is achievable. Moreover, the numerical KL example simultaneously treats the required bucket as uniform among 1,024 buckets and its best token as the globally second-most-likely token; that cannot hold for nearly all buckets. The perplexity proof evaluates only the likelihood of the base model's argmax token rather than standard cross-entropy over the base distribution, so labeling it a conventional perplexity bound is misleading.

The probing results do not yet validate an operational detector. Probes are trained with labeled secrets that are explicitly present in each prompt, and malicious models are compared primarily with untouched base models. There is no matched benign fine-tuning control, detector-level false-positive evaluation, or test across unrelated fine-tuned checkpoints. Thus the reported gap may reflect generic task-specific fine-tuning or increased processing of the prompt secret rather than a steganography-specific signature.

The strongest detection wording overstates inconsistent results. Under the non-decodable XOR control, bit-probe detection succeeds in only three of eight scenarios, and Ministral full fine-tuning often lacks clear separation. Higher embedding-regression cosine similarity is interesting but is not directly converted into a reliable model-level decision rule.

Practical attack effectiveness remains limited: representative LoRA exact-match rates are only 19–43%, OOD transfer depends strongly on the training prompt distribution, and several settings lose 10–30 percentage points on downstream capabilities. Experiments cover only four-letter, 32-bit secrets and therefore do not establish performance for realistic payload sizes or trigger frequencies.

Text-quality evidence is comparatively weak: coherence and stability use only 10 prompts per configuration, KL uses 20, and there is no human evaluation. Claims that quality shifts lie within normal fine-tuning ranges are therefore not convincingly established.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Hyperparameters and probe architecture are documented well, but important details such as recoverability-classifier dataset sizes and precise attack generation procedures are missing, and only detection code is promised for open release. Withholding attack code can be ethically justified, but it still limits independent verification. Overall, the attack experiments are promising, yet the unsupported security, theoretical, and detector-specificity claims require substantial revision before acceptance.
